To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the excess incidence of cancer in a screened group compared with an unscreened control group is not necessarily an unbiased estimate of overdiagnosis and that no trial or population study design automatically permits unbiased estimation.

(1) screening advances the date of clinical presentation for preclinical relevant cancers and (2) the extent of overdiagnosis is the difference in incidence between the screened and unscreened groups after the screening effect has stabilized.

(1) The excess incidence of relevant cancers in the screen group relative to the control group is not necessarily equal to the overdiagnosed incidence of relevant cancers; (2) The excess incidence in the screen group is a biased estimate of the overdiagnoses in the control group; and (3) The bias in the excess incidence is a function of the preclinical detectability of relevant cancers, the test sensitivity, the screening interval, and the screening patterns.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of overdiagnosis of cancer.
a problem that has been a topic of much debate in the medical literature, but for which there has been little mathematical or statistical work.
the problem of estimating overdiagnosis of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the incidence of overdiagnosis in a population setting is unknown and that it is not possible to estimate overdiagnosis in the population setting with a single study or trial design.
the overdiagnosis rate of prostate cancer is not known and that the excess incidence in screened men does not provide a reliable estimate.
the over-diagnosis rate of prostate cancer in the ERSPC is 48.6% (44.0–53.2) for the 50–69 years old age group, and that it increases with age to 55.5% (51.1–59.9) in the 70–74 years old age group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are no automatic conditions under which overdiagnosis can be measured accurately.
overdiagnosis is a real problem, but we don't know how big it is.
overdiagnosis can be estimated in randomized screening trials but that there are conditions to consider and that it is not as easy as many think.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the excess incidence in screened groups relative to unscreened groups is not necessarily a valid estimate of overdiagnosis.
excess incidence in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is not a valid empirical estimate of overdiagnosis.
there are no shortcuts.
